name: Protein intake for hair

lead: The idea is that because hair is made largely of keratin, eating enough protein supports hair growth and quality. It is discussed in the lifestyle sections of hair and looksmaxxing communities as a way to keep hair full and strong from the inside.

General hair-care references state that a balanced diet matters and that deficiencies often show first in hair, naming protein, iron, zinc, biotin and other nutrients as linked to dryness, shedding or weak hair. Dermatology references list malnutrition, B12 deficiency and iron deficiency among causes of non-scarring hair loss. No studies were found testing extra protein for hair in people with normal intake.

paras: People make sure meals include protein sources through the day, often alongside attention to iron, zinc and B12, and treat it as part of an overall diet rather than a standalone fix. Hair changes, if any, show up over months, since hair grows slowly.

References do not report specific harms from adequate protein intake. Hair-loss references note supplements are not typically recommended for hair loss and that there is no evidence for biotin; persistent shedding is a reason to see a clinician to check for deficiencies.

angle.text: Hair is largely keratin, so eating enough protein is meant to keep growth and hair quality on track. References link deficiency, rather than extra intake, to dryness, shedding and weak hair.

lead: Protein intake for hair is the idea that eating enough protein supports hair growth and quality, because hair is made largely of keratin. It is discussed in lifestyle sections of hair and looksmaxxing communities.

General hair-care references state that a balanced diet matters and that deficiencies often show first in hair, naming protein, iron, zinc, biotin and other nutrients as linked to dryness, shedding or weak hair, though much of that text is uncited.[1] The same reference says shampoos or vitamins have not been shown to noticeably change growth rate.[1]

Dermatology references list malnutrition, vitamin B12 deficiency and iron deficiency among causes of non-scarring hair loss, and state that supplements are not typically recommended for hair loss and that there is no evidence for biotin.[2]

sections.h: Reported links between nutrition and hair
paras: Hair-care references say deficiencies of nutrients including protein can appear in the hair, and that growth is about 1.25 cm per month.[1] Hair-loss references mention malnutrition and iron or B12 deficiency as less common non-scarring causes.[2]
A hair-loss reference says supplements are not typically recommended, and that for most alternative remedies evidence is insufficient.[2]
